objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how the eye finds and misses traffic, teach a learner a scan and clearing habit that fits every phase of flight and every light condition, tell whether the learner is really seeing traffic, and manage the collision risks of the training environment, including when you act as a safety pilot.
why: Every pilot must keep a lookout to see and avoid other aircraft whenever weather permits, IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. In one study of midair collisions a flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of the accidents [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. The habit you build on the first flight is the one your learners keep, which is why the AFH says to teach scanning at the very beginning of training [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

warmup: Think first: your learner's eyes are pointed out the windshield and they say "clear." A moment later you spot a low-wing airplane at 10 o'clock, a little high, that they never mentioned. What could explain the miss, and how would you find out whether they were looking or actually seeing, without simply taking over the scan yourself?

key_terms.def: The duty of every person operating an aircraft, IFR or VFR, to keep watch for and maneuver to avoid other aircraft when weather conditions permit [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]] [[16:2|AC 90-48E 6.1]].
The very small center area at the back of the eye that sends clear, sharply focused images to the brain [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].
Vision outside the central focus. It gives little detail but detects movement, usually the first sign of a collision threat [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].
Refocusing the eyes between near and far. It takes 1 to 2 seconds to go from a panel 2 feet away to an aircraft 1 mile away [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.4]].
With nothing to focus on, the eyes relax to a focal distance of about 10 to 30 feet; the pilot looks without seeing [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].
A target on a collision course seems to hang still and stay small for a long time, then suddenly fills a window [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]].
A maneuver, usually clearing turns, to be certain the next maneuver will not proceed into another aircraft's flightpath [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
A night technique: look about 10 degrees above, below or to either side of an object so the rods can keep it in view [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].
The optic disk, where the optic nerve meets the retina. It has no rods or cones, so each eye is blind there [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]].

The pilot in the other control seat during simulated instrument flight; at least a private pilot certificate with the right category and class, with adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]].
A cockpit display of traffic that helps you find other aircraft. It is not a collision avoidance system and does not relieve the see and avoid duty [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]].
TCAS I gives proximity warnings only; TCAS II adds resolution advisories, climb or descend [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16]].

chunks.title: K3: See and avoid, and the instructor's share

body.p: When weather conditions permit, every person operating an aircraft must maintain vigilance to see and avoid other aircraft, whether the flight is IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. The AIM says the same from the pilot and controller side: when conditions permit, the pilot sees and avoids traffic, terrain and obstacles regardless of flight plan or radar service [[34:6|AIM 5-5-8]]. Using a pattern, service or procedure never reduces that duty, from ramp-out to ramp-in [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].

bullets: VFR visibility and cloud clearance rules exist to help the pilot meet the see and avoid duty [[33:189|AIM 3-3-2]].
Controllers give radar traffic information only when workload permits [[34:6|AIM 5-5-8]], and it does not relieve the pilot of continual vigilance [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15]].

The number one cause of midair collisions is failure to follow the see and avoid concept [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.3]]. The NTSB names a pilot failing to see and avoid as the most probable cause [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].
No one may fly so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111(a)]].

body.p: Your share as an instructor: guard against becoming so busy teaching that you stop watching for traffic, and be especially alert in simulated instrument flight and with advanced avionics, where people tend to look inside too much [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]]. The Private ACS has the evaluator assess visual scanning and collision avoidance throughout the entire test, and other FAA guidance encourages CFIs to train and assess these skills [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.3]]. Flight instructors must train applicants to give collision avoidance maximum attention [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.1]].

callout.text: If learners believe you are doing all the looking, they never build the habit. From the first flight, make it clear that you are both responsible for the lookout [[25:181|AIH 9-11]] [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: During dual instruction, who does the AIH say is responsible for maintaining the lookout?
check.a: Both the instructor and the learner. Say it out loud so the learner does not hand the scan to you [[25:191|AIH 10-7]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

chunks.title: K4 and K6: How the eye finds traffic, and the cues of a collision course

body.p: The eyes take in about a 200 degree arc of the horizon at a glance, but only the fovea, a very small center area, sends sharp images to the brain [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. The eye can focus on and classify an object only within about 10 to 15 degrees, so pilots tend not to believe what they see out of the corner of the eye [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.7]].

head: Seen with
How close before it is recognized
rows: Foveal (central) vision
An aircraft about 7 miles away can be seen in sharp focus [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].
Outside foveal vision
The same aircraft must be about 7/10 of a mile away to be recognized [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].

body.p: Why peripheral vision matters (K4): it gives little detail, but it detects movement. Each time the scan stops and the eyes refocus, peripheral vision becomes more important, and apparent movement is usually the first perception of a collision threat, the discovery that starts the evasive action [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]. At night scanning depends almost entirely on peripheral vision [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]].
Visual cues of an impending midair collision (K6):

bullets: No relative motion: an aircraft that stays in one scan quadrant is likely on a collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8e]] [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].
No lateral or vertical motion but growing in size: take immediate evasive action [[24:32|AFH 1-11]] [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8e]].

The blossom effect: the target seems motionless and the same size for a long time, then suddenly blooms to fill a window. A large bug smear or dirty spot can hide it until too late [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]] [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]].
Relative altitude: an aircraft above the horizon is probably on a higher flight path; below the horizon, probably lower [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8b]].
At night: lights growing brighter mean the aircraft is approaching; dimming means it is moving away [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]].

callout.text: Still and growing means it is coming for you. Movement catches the eye, and a collision course has none.

check.q: A converging airplane appears just above the horizon. What does that suggest about its altitude?
check.a: It is probably on a higher flight path than yours [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8b]].

chunks.title: K4, S1 and S3: The scan itself

body.p: Effective scanning is a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements that bring successive areas of the sky into the central visual field. Each movement should be no more than 10 degrees, and each area should be watched for at least 1 second to allow detection [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]] [[16:12|AC 90-48E 12]]. Most pilots prefer horizontal back-and-forth movements, but each pilot should develop a comfortable pattern and stick to it [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

head: Technique
How
Source
rows: Side-to-side scan
Sweep the sky in steps of 10 degrees or less, at least 1 second per area, covering the windshield and the side windows.
Start left, finish right
The brain already processes sight information left to right, so begin over the left shoulder and move across the windshield to the right.
Panel-to-outside path

From the panel, look along the left wing past the tip to the center of the first quadrant. After the sweep, come back in along the right wing from its tip, then start the panel scan. This reduces eye fatigue.
Shift and refocus
The eyes focus somewhere even in a featureless sky, so shift glances and refocus at intervals.
Whole sky
Scan the entire sky and try not to focus straight ahead.
Night: far to near
Scan side to side, starting at the greatest distance and moving inward. Each stop covers about 30 degrees, lasts no longer than 2 to 3 seconds, and overlaps the last by 10 degrees.
Night: off-center viewing
Look about 10 degrees above, below or to either side of a dim object, with short stops.

callout.text: Appropriate technique (S3) means matching the scan to the conditions: 10 degree steps of at least 1 second by day, off-center viewing with short stops at night, and deliberate refocusing on distant objects whenever the sky is empty [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]] [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]] [[1:444|PHAK 17-22]].

check.q: Where does the AIM suggest the eyes go first when leaving the panel to begin the outside scan?
check.a: Along the left wing, past the wingtip, to the center of the first scan quadrant [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].

chunks.title: K1: Environmental conditions that degrade vision

body.p: In flight, vision is affected by atmospheric conditions, glare, lighting, windshield deterioration and distortion, aircraft design, cabin temperature, oxygen supply (particularly at night) and acceleration forces [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.1]].

head: Condition
Effect
What to teach
rows: Haze
Alters how aircraft look; even at the VFR 5 statute miles a pilot may struggle to detect traffic [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]].
AC 90-48E recommends flying above a haze layer [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]].
Smoke, dust and rain
Greatly reduce the ability to detect targets [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8i]].
Check the weather for smoke, haze and precipitation before the flight [[16:8|AC 90-48E 9.3]].
Sun and glare
Flying into the sun, glare often hides the other aircraft; with the sun behind you, traffic stands out. Worst over a sunlit cloud layer [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.10]].
Plan for the time of day and sun direction [[16:8|AC 90-48E 9.4]]. Sunglasses should absorb at least 85 percent of visible light, all colors equally [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6b]].
Dirty or scratched windshield
Greatly reduces the ability to see traffic and worsens glare [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8h]] [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.10]].
Keep it clean, every flight [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8h]].
Featureless sky above clouds or in haze
Eyes relax to 10 to 30 feet: looking without seeing [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].
Focus on distant objects or light sources [[1:444|PHAK 17-22]].
Dim light and night

Another aircraft must be much closer to be seen unless its navigation lights are on. Full dark adaptation needs at least 30 minutes, and a bright light undoes it in seconds [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6b]]. Ground lights make traffic harder to pick out [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]].
Protect dark adaptation; keep interior lights low [[34:189|AIM 8-1-8k]].
Altitude
Dark adaptation is impaired above 5,000 feet cabin pressure altitude [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6b]]; night vision declines measurably above 4,000 feet without oxygen [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]].
Consider oxygen at night even where not required [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]].
Reduced in-flight visibility
Raises the risk of not seeing conflicting traffic [[16:14|AC 90-48E 14.2]].
Avoid inadvertent VFR into IMC with good weather planning [[16:14|AC 90-48E 14.2]].

body.p: The pilot's condition matters too: scanning is easily degraded by fatigue, boredom, illness, anxiety or preoccupation [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]. Alcohol leads pilots to stare at objects and neglect scanning, and exhausted pilots fixate on instruments or stare off [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]].

callout.text: Make vision a preflight item: the AC lists weather (smoke, haze, precipitation) and time of day (sun glare, night lighting) as things that affect your ability to see and avoid [[16:8|AC 90-48E 9.3]] [[16:8|AC 90-48E 9.4]].

check.q: A learner plans a westbound flight late on a hazy afternoon. Name two vision threats to brief.
check.a: Glare from flying toward the sun, which can hide traffic [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.10]] [[16:8|AC 90-48E 9.4]], and haze, which makes traffic hard to detect even at legal visibility [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]].

chunks.title: K2: Vestibular and visual illusions while you scan

body.p: Illusions rank among the most common factors cited in fatal accidents [[34:184|AIM 8-1-5a]]. In visual conditions the eyes usually win over false sensations from the inner ear; take away the visual cues and false sensations can quickly disorient a pilot [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. Scanning keeps the head and eyes moving, so teach the illusions that interact with it.

head: Illusion
Type
Link to scanning
rows: Coriolis illusion
Vestibular

An abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn can create the feeling of rotation in a different axis, the most overwhelming illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5b]]. Teach minimal, smooth head movement, especially when retrieving objects [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
The leans
Vestibular

A turn entered so gradually that the inner ear misses it (the PHAK puts the detection threshold at a rotational acceleration of 2 degrees per second or lower) feels level; leveling the wings then feels like a bank the other way [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]] [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5b]].
False horizon
Visual
Sloping clouds, an obscured horizon, or ground lights and stars can make the pilot misalign the aircraft with the real horizon [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5b]] [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].
Autokinesis
Visual
A static light stared at in the dark appears to move after about 8 to 10 seconds. Visual scanning is the most important cure; do not stare at a light for more than 10 seconds [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]].
Reversible perspective
Visual (night)

Another aircraft may seem to move away when it is approaching, often when flying a parallel course. Watch its lights and their position relative to the horizon [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]] [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]].
Fascination (fixation)
Visual and attention
Attention locks on one goal or object; students do it on the instruments or while landing and forget what is around them [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]].

body.p: Teaching tool: the PHAK describes in-flight demonstrations of disorientation, such as climbing while turning, tilting and reversal of motion. They show how false bodily sensations can be and build trust in the instruments. Never do them at low altitude or without an instructor or appropriate safety pilot [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

callout.text: Head-down tasks in a long turn are a coriolis setup. If something is dropped, retrieve it with minimal head movement [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]], and save "pick up the chart" style distractions for straight flight.

check.q: The PHAK gives three ways to reduce autokinesis. Which is the most important?
check.a: Visual scanning. The others are more lights or varying the light intensity [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]].

chunks.title: K5 and S2: Blind spots and scanning around them

body.p: Fixed structure hides parts of the sky. High-wing airplanes restrict the view above, low-wing airplanes the view below, and the worst case is a low-wing airplane flying above a high-wing airplane [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]] [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. The AIM adds windshield posts, sun visors, and the blind spots the airplane's attitude creates [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

Why the head must move (S2): each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve meets the retina. With both eyes open this is no problem, because an object cannot be in both blind spots at once. But when a windshield divider blocks one eye's view, a target can fall in the other eye's blind spot and go unseen [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]]. An object seen by only one eye can also blur, so move your head, not just your eyes, around obstructions [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.6]].

bullets: Move the head to see around door posts and wings; at times maneuver, for example lift a wing [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8j]].
Remove curtains and stow loose items such as maps on the glare shield [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8j]].
Climb: adjust the pitch attitude to improve the view over the nose [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].
Cruise or descent: gentle shallow banks left and right, and check behind by scanning from behind the right wing, through the windscreen, to the back of the left wing [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].
In the pattern, keep checking blind spots and look to the rear occasionally; banking now and then uncovers blind spots [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

check.q: Your learner holds the head still and darts the eyes at the left door post. What does AC 90-48E want instead, and why?
check.a: Move the head. An object hidden from one eye by a post can blur or be missed, and the other eye's blind spot may cover it [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.6]] [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]].

body.p: The idea of a clearing turn is to be certain the next maneuver will not proceed into another aircraft's flightpath. Some programs require two 90 degree turns in opposite directions before any training maneuver; instructors may develop other methods. Whatever you choose, teach an effective procedure, insist on it, and have the learner clear before all turns and every training maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

head: When
Clearing procedure
rows: Before takeoff
Before taxiing onto the runway, scan the approach areas for landing traffic and maneuver to get a clear view of them [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15a]].
Climbs and descents
Gentle banks left and right at a frequency that allows continuous scanning [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15b]].
Straight and level
Break long periods at intervals with clearing procedures [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15c]].
Traffic pattern
Avoid entering while descending [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15d]].
VORs and airway intersections
Sustained vigilance, because traffic converges there [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15e]].
Before a turn, high-wing airplane
Momentarily raise the wing toward the turn and look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f]].
Before a turn, low-wing airplane
Momentarily lower the wing toward the turn and look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f]].
Before maneuvers
Clear before all turns, chandelles, lazy eights, stalls, slow flight, climbs, spins and combination maneuvers [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f]].

callout.text: Have the learner verbalize it: "clear left, right, above and below" [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]] [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15f]]. Saying it builds and keeps the habit, and it lets you hear whether the clearing happened.

body.p: Clearing combined with proper scanning is the most effective collision avoidance strategy [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

check.q: What does the AFH say makes clearing procedures the most effective collision avoidance strategy?
check.a: Combining them with proper visual scanning technique [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

chunks.title: K7 and R3: Where and when the risk is greatest

body.p: Most midair collisions and reported near midair collisions happen in good VFR weather, in daylight, within 5 miles of an airport and/or near navigation aids [[24:31|AFH 1-10]].

bullets: In the airport traffic pattern, final and the runway each account for 34 percent of midair collisions, downwind and short final 16 percent each [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

56 percent happen in the afternoon, 32 percent in the morning and 2 percent at night, dusk or dawn. A collision is most likely between two aircraft going the same direction, and nearly all happen at or near uncontrolled airports below 1,000 feet [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

Most aircraft in collisions were flying recreationally without a flight plan, mostly on weekend daylight hours with visibility over 3 miles; pilots from first solo to 20,000 hours were involved [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
Airways, especially near VORs, and Class B, C, D and E surface areas are where aircraft cluster [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8f]].

26.6 percent of fatal accidents in the last 10 years occurred during maneuvering flight, and the maneuvers take attention from scanning. Formation and air tour flying have produced midair collisions too [[16:12|AC 90-48E 11.2.2]] [[16:4|AC 90-48E 7.2]].
Training areas are often crowded and hazy, and practice approaches without ATC surveillance concentrate aircraft along the same path [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

body.p: High volume operational environments (R3): as traffic density and closing speeds increase, the collision risk rises and scanning matters more [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1]]. A radar environment still requires vigilance [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8f]]. Mitigations to teach: use ATC support whenever possible [[34:189|AIM 8-1-8l]]; exterior lights on, day or night [[34:189|AIM 8-1-8k]]; descend to pattern altitude before entering, keep a constant scan, and expect aircraft without radios [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]; and plan the flight on the ground so less time goes to heads-down tasks [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8g]].

callout.text: The clear Saturday afternoon near a non-towered field is the classic midair setting, not the marginal day [[24:31|AFH 1-10]] [[24:170|AFH 8-6]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: On which two parts of the traffic pattern does AFH Figure 8-4 put the most midair collisions?
check.a: Final and the runway, 34 percent each [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

chunks.title: K8 and R1: Dividing attention and managing distractions

body.p: The chance of spotting a threat rises with time spent looking outside, so the pilot must timeshare between scanning the sky and monitoring the instruments [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6c]].

head: Guideline
What it says
rows: AIM inside and outside split
Time on visual tasks inside should be no more than 1/4 to 1/3 of the time spent outside: about 4 to 5 seconds on the panel for every 16 seconds outside [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].
AFH integrated flight instruction
About 90 percent of attention on outside references and scanning for traffic, with quick checks of the instruments [[24:66|AFH 3-5]].
Refocus cost
1 to 2 seconds from a panel 2 feet away to an aircraft 1 mile away [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.4]]; the AIM says it may take several seconds [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].
Cockpit management
Study maps, checklists and frequencies before flight so less time is needed inside [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8g]].

body.p: Distractions to visual scanning (R1):

bullets: Concentration on flight instruments or tablets, and passengers [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].
New avionics that cause fixation on displays and draw attention inside [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15]].
Checklists or unnecessary conversation while taxiing [[16:8|AC 90-48E 10.1.2]].
Maneuvering, formation flying, and duties like narrating a tour [[16:12|AC 90-48E 11.2.2]] [[16:4|AC 90-48E 7.2]].
A minor problem, such as a gauge reading wrong, that becomes an accident as attention shifts to it [[25:17|AIH 1-13]].

Your own teaching: too much coaching on final can cause missed calls and less attention to collision avoidance, so use concise prompts [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Do most takeoff teaching before calling the tower or announcing on CTAF [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

callout.text: Test division of attention: ask where the other traffic in the pattern is, or invent a problem with a radio. If the learner lets it pull them off the scan, point out that situational awareness was lost [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

check.q: Where does the AIH say an instructor should do most of the teaching for a takeoff, and why?
check.a: Before contacting the tower or announcing on CTAF, to avoid overloading the learner, keep a sterile flight deck and support collision avoidance [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

chunks.title: R2 and R4: Relaxed focus and collision reaction time

body.p: Relaxed intermediate focal distance (R2): with nothing to focus on, as above clouds or in a haze layer, the eyes relax to a comfortable focal distance of 10 to 30 feet. The pilot is looking without seeing [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. It usually happens on vague, colorless days with no distinct horizon [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.5]].

bullets: Effective scanning helps prevent it [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. Shift glances and refocus at intervals, and focus outside to set up the eyes for detecting targets [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].
Search out and focus on distant objects or light sources, however dim [[1:444|PHAK 17-22]].
Consider flying above the haze layer [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]].

body.p: Collision reaction time (R4): AC 90-48E Table 1 adds up the time from first seeing an object until the airplane starts to move.

head: Event
Seconds
rows: See object
Recognize aircraft
Become aware of collision course
Decision to turn left or right
Muscular reaction
Aircraft lag time
Total before the aircraft begins to move

body.p: Add the 1 to 2 seconds the eyes need to refocus from the panel [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.4]], and remember that high closure rates limit the time for detection, decision and evasive action [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]. When you do maneuver, expect the other pilot may be maneuvering too: watch the other aircraft, then resume scanning, since there may be more traffic [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8d]]. Know the right-of-way rules so you can act at once, preferably in compliance with them [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8c]].

callout.text: Twelve and a half seconds before the airplane even starts to move. Find them early or you may not find them in time.

check.q: Which single event in AC 90-48E Table 1 takes the longest?
check.a: Becoming aware of the collision course, 5.0 seconds [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]].

body.p: Electronic systems help you find traffic; none replaces your eyes. Air traffic information equipment does not relieve the regulatory duty to see and avoid [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15]].

head: System
What it does
Limits
rows: ADS-B In traffic display

An effective aid; many units add visual or audio alerts. Make the display part of the normal scan; before entering or crossing a runway it can show arriving and pattern traffic [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

Aircraft without ADS-B Out or a transponder will not show [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]]. Not a collision avoidance system; no avoidance maneuvers based on the display, and none without visual contact [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]].
TIS-B
Ground broadcast of radar-derived traffic to ADS-B equipped aircraft, filling in aircraft without ADS-B Out [[33:305|AIM 4-5-8c]].
Only transponder-equipped targets; no radar coverage means no TIS-B, and low-altitude coverage near some airports is limited [[33:305|AIM 4-5-8c]].
TIS
Proximity warning to help you visually acquire intruders [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17]].
No avoidance maneuvers authorized from it; misses aircraft without transponders or outside radar coverage [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17]].
TCAS I
Proximity warning only, to help visual acquisition [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16a]].
No avoidance maneuvers provided or authorized [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16a]].
TCAS II
Traffic advisories plus resolution advisories, vertical only (climb or descend) [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16b]].
On a TA, look for the traffic but do not deviate from a clearance on TA information alone [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16b]]. It does not see aircraft without working transponders [[33:288|AIM 4-4-16]].
ATC radar traffic information
Calls on targets that may come close, so you can look for them [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15a]].
Limited by radar, traffic volume, workload and frequency congestion [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15b]]; do not depend on it alone [[16:14|AC 90-48E 16]].

bullets: A "traffic in sight" reply must be based on seeing the aircraft out the window, not on the cockpit display [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17d]].
Systems with a traffic alerting feature help reduce the urge to fixate on the display; limit time spent focused on instruments or tablets [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

ADS-B Out, not In, is what 14 CFR 91.225 requires in the listed airspace [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225]]. The FAA also recommends anticollision strobes, pulse lights, dual radios and traffic systems [[16:13|AC 90-48E 14]] [[16:14|AC 90-48E 14]].

body.p: Teaching angle: teach new avionics on the ground first, covering features, limitations, and the pitfalls of fixation and overreliance [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]]. Know the avionics yourself before you instruct in them [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: Which TCAS gives resolution advisories, and in what direction?
check.a: TCAS II. Its resolution advisories are vertical only, climb or descend [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16b]].

chunks.title: R5: The safety pilot and the instructor as lookout

body.p: Simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot in the other control seat holding at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft (a narrow sport pilot instructor exception applies only to solo cross-country training). The safety pilot must have adequate vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer must supplement it, and the airplane needs fully functioning dual controls, with a limited throwover-wheel exception [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(3)]].

bullets: A pilot logging approaches for instrument currency records the safety pilot's name, if one was required [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)(ii)]].

Choose weather good enough to make up for the safety pilot's restricted view and the flying pilot's attention on the instruments, with extra margin near busy airways or airports [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16c]].
Safety pilots and instructors should guard against preoccupation and watch hardest during simulated instrument flight, when the tendency is to look inside [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].
Spatial disorientation demonstrations need an instructor or appropriate safety pilot and enough altitude [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

body.p: Application: with the flying pilot under a view-limiting device, the lookout rests on the safety pilot. Brief before the flight how traffic will be called and how control will change hands, using the three-step positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: A safety pilot who is chatting, teaching the approach or programming the GPS is not a lookout. Preoccupation is the first thing AC 90-48E tells instructors and safety pilots to guard against [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

check.q: What minimum certificate must the safety pilot hold for your instrument student's hood work in a single-engine land airplane?
check.a: At least a private pilot certificate with airplane category and single-engine land class ratings [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)(i)]].

body.p: Start on the first flight. Collision avoidance, with proper scanning and clearing procedures, is a basic safety practice to emphasize beginning with the very first dual flight [[24:31|AFH 1-10]], and visual scanning should be taught at the very beginning of training [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

head: Step
What you do
rows: Explanation (ground)

Objectives and standard; how the fovea and peripheral vision work; the 10 degree, 1 second scan; your airplane's blind spots; the clearing procedure you will insist on [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Run the PHAK blind spot demonstration with Figure 17-15 [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]] [[1:444|PHAK 17-22]].
Instructor tells, instructor does
Narrate your own scan and clearing aloud. Learners imitate the instructor, so demonstrate exactly the way they should practice, including the safety procedures [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner talks you through the scan and calls traffic while you fly [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Learner tells and does
The learner flies, scans and calls "clear left, right, above and below" before each maneuver [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15f]].
Learner does, instructor evaluates
Watch quietly; note whether the learner found the traffic you saw; debrief with the learner's own assessment first [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

body.p: How to tell whether a learner is really looking: follow their eyes. A long stare at one instrument suggests fixation; a gaze that never reaches some area suggests inattention. But looking in the same direction is not the same as seeing [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. So test the result too: ask where the other traffic in the pattern is [[25:18|AIH 1-14]], and prompt the learner to name collision hazards before a maneuver [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Application: when you spot traffic first, ask "what do you see at 10 o'clock?" before you point.

bullets: Make clearing part of every maneuver, and correct at once any entry without a traffic check [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
Use integrated flight instruction: outside references first, instruments in quick checks [[24:66|AFH 3-5]].

Teach the traffic display on the ground first, features and limits [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]]. In flight, have the learner find each displayed target out the window, since "in sight" means out the window [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17d]].

callout.text: Model it every time. Learners treat the instructor as a role model, and safety practices you describe but do not demonstrate mean little [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

check.q: Why is following the learner's eyes not enough to prove they saw the traffic?
check.a: Looking in the same direction is not the same as seeing what the instructor sees [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]; ask them to report the traffic.

body.p: Each row is an error the sources name or warn against. Use the middle column to spot it and the right column to fix it.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Entering maneuvers without clearing
The learner rolls into a turn or stall setup with no look around.
Correct it immediately and require the clearing procedure before every turn and maneuver [[25:181|AIH 9-11]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
Not scanning during the maneuver
Clearing done, then eyes locked on the maneuver.
Steep turn error lists include both not clearing and failing to scan during the maneuver [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]; prompt a look mid-maneuver.
Fixation on one instrument or display
Eyes parked on one gauge or the tablet for a long time.
Point it out [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]; limit time on instruments and tablets [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].
Staring straight ahead
The head never turns past the windshield posts.
Scan the entire sky and do not focus straight ahead [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].
Moving only the eyes around posts
Head still, eyes darting at a door post.
Looking without seeing
A fixed, distant gaze into empty sky above haze or clouds.
Refocus on distant objects at intervals [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]] [[1:444|PHAK 17-22]].
Trusting the traffic display
"No traffic" because the screen is empty, or "traffic in sight" from the screen.
Aircraft without ADS-B Out or transponders do not show, and "in sight" means out the window [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]] [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17d]].
Descending into the pattern
Joining downwind while still descending.
Descend to pattern altitude before entering [[24:170|AFH 8-6]] [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15d]].
Heads-down tasks while taxiing
Checklist in the lap while rolling.
Do checklists before taxi and keep eyes outside [[16:8|AC 90-48E 10.1.2]].
Leaving the lookout to the instructor
The learner stops calling traffic when you are aboard.
Make the lookout shared and expected [[25:181|AIH 9-11]] [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: A learner finishes the clearing turns, starts steep turns and never looks outside for traffic again. Which AFH-listed error is this?
check.a: Failure to scan for other traffic during the maneuver [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

Right: a photo of a cockpit labeled Windshield, with a yellow loop across the panel and windshield and red curved arrows out to each side window.

Demonstration-performance: explanation, demonstration, learner performance and instructor supervision, evaluation. Telling-and-doing: preparation; instructor tells, instructor does; learner tells, instructor does; learner tells, learner does; learner does, instructor evaluates.

scenario.title: Hood work on a busy Saturday
scenario.setup: You are the CFI and safety pilot for an instrument student flying practice approaches under a view-limiting device in a high-wing trainer with an ADS-B In tablet. The airport is non-towered, about 4 miles from a Class C surface area. It is a clear Saturday afternoon with a haze layer topping out near 6,000 feet, and the CTAF is busy with pattern traffic.

questions.q: Are you legal as the safety pilot, and what must you be able to see?
questions.a: Yes, if you hold at least a private certificate with airplane single-engine land ratings. You need adequate vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer to supplement it [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

questions.q: Why is this setting high risk for a midair?
questions.a: Good VFR weather, daylight and within 5 miles of an airport [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]; a non-towered field below 1,000 feet on a weekend [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]; and practice approaches without ATC surveillance concentrate aircraft on one path [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: The student asks you to check the approach setup and you both look at the panel for about 20 seconds. What went wrong?
questions.a: Preoccupation during instruction, the first thing AC 90-48E tells safety pilots to guard against [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]]. Inside time should be about 4 to 5 seconds per 16 outside [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. Help briefly, then go back to the scan.

questions.q: Level at 3,000 feet under the haze, you catch yourself gazing at a blank sky. What is happening and what do you do?
questions.a: Empty-field myopia: the eyes relax to 10 to 30 feet and you look without seeing [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. Shift glances and refocus at intervals [[24:32|AFH 1-11]] and pick out distant objects to focus on [[1:444|PHAK 17-22]].

questions.q: The tablet shows a target 2 miles ahead that you cannot see. Can you maneuver on the display, and what else helps?
questions.a: No. The display only assists visual acquisition; no avoidance maneuvers are authorized from it [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]]. Keep looking, use ATC traffic support where available [[34:189|AIM 8-1-8l]], and never report it in sight from the screen [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17d]].

questions.q: On final you spot a Cub on base, converging with no relative motion and growing. How much time do you have, and what do you do?
questions.a: Table 1 needs 12.5 seconds before the airplane even begins to move [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]], so act now: no relative motion and growing means immediate evasive action [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]. Take the controls with a positive exchange [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], watch the Cub, then resume scanning [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8d]].

skills.do: Effectively scan using short regularly spaced eye movements: from the right seat, scan aloud in moves of no more than 10 degrees, pausing at least 1 second per area, while explaining why (only the fovea gives sharp vision) [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. The CFI ACS gives no numeric tolerance for this Task; the examiner judges the scan and your explanation.
skills.practice: On every flight, narrate one full sweep after each panel scan and check yourself against about 4 to 5 seconds inside for each 16 seconds outside [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].

skills.do: Scan around physical obstructions: show moving the head around door posts and wings, raising or lowering a wing, and checking behind, and explain the binocular blind spot reason [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.6]] [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8j]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f]].
skills.practice: Sit in each airplane you teach in, find its posts, wing and visor blind spots, and plan how you will show each one [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

skills.do: Use appropriate visual scanning techniques: pick and explain the technique for the phase and conditions, such as clearing turns before maneuvers, gentle banks in climbs and descents, pitch changes in the climb, and off-center viewing at night [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]] [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].
skills.practice: Fly a practice lesson where you call each technique by name as you use it, including "clear left, right, above and below" [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

skills.do: Use electronic traffic alert systems, if available: brief the system's features and limits, include the display in the scan, use it to find traffic out the window, and never maneuver on it or call traffic in sight from it alone [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]] [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]] [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17d]].
skills.practice: With the avionics manual, practice the ground briefing you would give a learner on the unit's alerts and what it cannot show [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

quiz.q: AC 90-48E names the number one cause of midair collisions as:
options: Night operations near airports
Air traffic control errors
Transponder failures in flight
Failure to adhere to the see and avoid concept
quiz.why: Failure to follow see and avoid is the number one cause [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.3]].

quiz.q: An aircraft in sharp focus at 7 miles with foveal vision must be about how close to be recognized outside foveal vision?
options: About 3.5 miles
2 miles
7/10 of a mile
1/10 of a mile

quiz.q: Why does the AIM suggest starting the outside scan over the left shoulder?
options: The brain is already trained to process sight information from left to right
Under the right-of-way rules, traffic on the left always has priority over you
Most traffic approaches from the left, so look there before the right
The left seat gives the widest view, so the scan should start there
quiz.why: The brain already processes visual information left to right [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].

quiz.q: Sunglasses for glare protection should absorb at least what share of visible light?
options: 85 percent
70 percent
50 percent
95 to 100 percent
quiz.why: At least 85 percent (15 percent transmittance), all colors equally [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6b]].

quiz.q: Staring at a single light at night, apparent movement (autokinesis) begins after about:
options: 1 to 2 seconds
8 to 10 seconds
About 30 seconds
2 minutes

quiz.q: In a climb, what does AC 90-48E suggest for seeing traffic ahead?
options: Look only out the side windows, never over the nose
Make steep turns of 45 degrees each way during the climb
Adjust the pitch attitude to see better over the nose
Rely on ATC traffic calls until reaching cruise altitude
quiz.why: Adjusting pitch improves visibility over the nose in a climb [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, a midair collision is most likely between two aircraft:
options: Approaching head-on
Crossing at right angles
One climbing and one descending
Going in the same direction
quiz.why: Most likely between two aircraft going the same direction [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

quiz.q: In integrated flight instruction, about how much of the pilot's attention does the AFH put outside?
options: 90 percent
75 percent
100 percent
50 percent
quiz.why: Approximately 90 percent outside on visual references and traffic [[24:66|AFH 3-5]].

quiz.q: In AC 90-48E Table 1, how long is the aircraft lag time?
options: 12.5 seconds
2.0 seconds
1.0 second
4.0 seconds
quiz.why: Aircraft lag time is 2.0 seconds [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]].

quiz.q: Under 91.109(c), a safety pilot's view may be supplemented by:
options: A traffic display with alerts
A competent observer in the aircraft
ATC radar traffic service
A mirror on the glare shield
quiz.why: A competent observer in the aircraft can supplement the safety pilot's vision [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is about to start a long descent from cruise in a high-wing trainer. What clearing does the AIM recommend during the descent?
options: Hold a steady straight descent so the attitude stays stable
One 360 degree clearing turn at the start, then straight ahead
Look only ahead over the nose, since that is where the traffic is
Gentle banks left and right, often enough to allow continuous scanning
final_quiz.why: Gentle banks left and right during climbs and descents [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15b]].

final_quiz.q: During slow flight you notice your learner has looked only at the airspeed indicator for many seconds. What does the AIH suggest this may be?
options: Inattention
Fixation
Complacency
Hypoxia
final_quiz.why: Looking at one instrument for an extended time suggests fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

final_quiz.q: On a night lesson your learner stares at a dim light to decide whether it is moving. What should you teach?
options: Stare at it longer, holding the eyes still until you are sure it moves
Look straight at it with one eye closed to remove the blind spot
Turn up the cockpit lights so the eyes adjust to the brighter scene
Look about 10 degrees to the side with short stops; keep scanning
final_quiz.why: Off-center viewing about 10 degrees away with short stops [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]] [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]]; staring causes autokinesis [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]].

final_quiz.q: What does the PHAK say alcohol and exhaustion do to a pilot's night scan?
options: Alcohol sharpens night vision for a while, but exhaustion blurs it
Only alcohol affects the scan; exhaustion affects reaction time only
Both lead pilots to stare at objects or fixate instead of scanning
Neither affects scanning; both only slow down dark adaptation
final_quiz.why: Pilots impaired by alcohol are likely to stare at objects and neglect scanning techniques, and exhausted pilots may get fixated on the instruments or stare off rather than multitask [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks when the examiner will grade visual scanning and collision avoidance on the private checkride. What does AC 90-48E say?
options: Only during the clearing turns before each flight maneuver
Throughout the entire test, as a safety of flight item
Only in the traffic pattern, where most collisions happen
Only during the oral, since it is a knowledge element
final_quiz.why: The Private Pilot ACS, Appendix 6, Safety of Flight, requires the evaluator to assess the applicant's visual scanning and collision avoidance procedures throughout the entire test [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.3]].

final_quiz.q: At a non-towered airport your learner wants to rely on ADS-B In to decide whether it is safe to take the runway. What do you teach?
options: Rely on it fully, since every aircraft near the airport must now appear on the display
Do not use ADS-B on the ground at all, because it only works once airborne
Only listen on CTAF; a traffic display is not allowed for runway decisions
Use it, but aircraft without ADS-B Out or a transponder won't show, so scan final too
final_quiz.why: ADS-B In can give advance notice before entering a runway, but aircraft without ADS-B Out or transponders do not show [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]]; scan the final, base and downwind and the runway [[16:9|AC 90-48E 10.2.2]].

final_quiz.q: After turning away from converging traffic, what should the learner do next according to the AIM?
options: Watch the other aircraft as it may maneuver too, then resume scanning for others
Return to the original maneuver at once, since the conflict is now resolved
Call ATC to report a near midair collision before doing anything else
Turn off the strobes so the other pilot is not blinded during the turn
final_quiz.why: Anticipate the other pilot maneuvering, watch it, then resume scanning [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8d]].

final_quiz.q: As safety pilot, you lean over to help reprogram the student's GPS approach for a long time. What does AC 90-48E warn about?
options: Nothing: during hood work the student pilot is the one responsible for the lookout
Wake turbulence from following the approach path of larger aircraft
Preoccupation, and looking inside too much in simulated instrument flight
Radio congestion from too many calls on the approach frequency
final_quiz.why: Guard against preoccupation, especially in simulated instrument flight [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

final_quiz.q: Why can a target go unseen when a windshield divider blocks one eye's view?
options: The divider causes glare that washes out the target
The target can fall in the other eye's blind spot
It triggers empty-field myopia in the uncovered eye
It causes the coriolis illusion when the head moves
final_quiz.why: With one eye blocked, a target can fall in the other eye's blind spot [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]]; move the head [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.6]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner first spends 3 seconds inside after 30 seconds outside, then 12 seconds inside after 16 seconds outside. Which breaks the AIM guideline?
options: Only the second
Only the first
Both
Neither of them breaks it
final_quiz.why: The AIM allows about 4 to 5 seconds inside per 16 outside. 3 of 30 fits; 12 of 16 does not [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].

final_quiz.q: Approach calls traffic at 2 o'clock. Your learner sees the target on the tablet and wants to reply "traffic in sight." What does the AIM say?
options: The reply must come from seeing it out the window, not from the display
That is fine, since an ADS-B target on a certified display counts as a sighting
That is fine for VFR flights, but IFR flights must see it out the window
Reply "traffic on the screen" instead, which ATC treats the same as in sight
final_quiz.why: A traffic-in-sight reply to ATC must be based on seeing an aircraft out the window, not on the cockpit display [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17d]].

final_quiz.q: A learner wants to practice maneuvers right over a VOR because it is easy to find. What is the risk?
options: None, since a VOR is an easy landmark that keeps the learner oriented
The VOR signal can interfere with the radios at close range
VORs always sit inside restricted airspace that needs a clearance
Traffic converges at VORs and airway intersections, so it needs constant vigilance
final_quiz.why: Traffic converges at VORs and intersections [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15e]]; aircraft cluster near VORs [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8f]].

final_quiz.q: At night, another aircraft seems to be moving away but its lights keep getting brighter. What is happening?
options: It is climbing away from you
It is moving away; its strobes just came on
It is approaching; this is the reversible perspective illusion
It is turning to land somewhere
final_quiz.why: Brighter lights mean approaching; the reversible perspective illusion can make it seem to move away [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]] [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]].

takeaways: See and avoid applies to every pilot, IFR or VFR, whenever weather permits, and you and the learner share the lookout.
Scan in moves of 10 degrees or less, at least 1 second per area; only the small foveal area sees sharply.
No relative motion plus growing size means a collision course; act now.
Move the head around posts, bank to uncover blind spots, and clear before every turn and maneuver.
Most midairs happen on good days, in daylight, near airports, especially on final and the runway.
Traffic displays and ATC calls help you look; they never replace looking.
Watch the learner's eyes, but test whether they actually see the traffic.
cfi_notes: The sources split inside and outside time differently: the AIM allows inside time up to 1/4 to 1/3 of outside time (4 to 5 seconds per 16) [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]], while the AFH's integrated flight instruction puts about 90 percent of attention outside [[24:66|AFH 3-5]]. Teach the AIM ratio as the ceiling and the AFH figure as the goal in visual flight.

Day and night scan stops differ: by day, moves of 10 degrees or less and at least 1 second per area [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]; at night the PHAK uses stops about 30 degrees wide, no longer than 2 to 3 seconds, overlapping 10 degrees [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]], and AC 90-48E says short stops of a few seconds [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]]. Teach them as two techniques.

Off-center viewing angle varies: the PHAK says 5 to 10 degrees in one place [[1:444|PHAK 17-22]] and 10 degrees in the next [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]]; AC 90-48E says approximately 10 degrees [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]].

Refocus time: AC 90-48E says 1 to 2 seconds [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.4]]; the AIM and AFH say several seconds [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]] [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]. Use the longer figure when you brief the cost of a heads-down glance.

Night vision and altitude: the AIM says dark adaptation is impaired above 5,000 feet cabin pressure altitude [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6b]]; the PHAK says night vision declines measurably above 4,000 feet without oxygen [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]].

AC 90-48E's list of recommended safety equipment says "ADS-B In and display capability, required as of January 1, 2020" [[16:14|AC 90-48E 14]], which reads as if ADS-B In were required. It is not: 14 CFR 91.225, in force since January 1, 2020, requires ADS-B Out equipment in the listed airspace and nothing requires In [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]]. The AC's own background paragraph also points to 91.225 for the requirement [[16:4|AC 90-48E 7.1]]. Teach the regulation: ADS-B In is recommended, ADS-B Out is required where 91.225 says.

AC 90-48E quotes a military pamphlet that cites "FAR Part 91.413" for operating the transponder [[16:4|AC 90-48E 7.3]]. The operating rule is 14 CFR 91.215(c), which refers to transponders maintained under 91.413 [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(c)]]. Teach 91.215(c).
Instructor tip (application): when you see traffic first, ask the learner what they see in that sector before pointing. It tests seeing, not just looking [[25:82|AIH 3-31]] [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

The CFI ACS gives no numeric standard for this Task. AC 90-48E notes that the Private ACS has the evaluator assess scanning and collision avoidance throughout the whole test [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.3]], so grade the habit on every flight, not just one lesson.
gaps: No source sets one required clearing procedure; two 90 degree turns is one example and programs differ [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. Follow your school's procedures or set your own and insist on it.
The blind spots of a specific airplane are not in these sources; sit in it and find them, and check the POH/AFM for visibility notes.
How a specific ADS-B In, TAS or TCAS unit alerts and displays traffic comes from its avionics manual or AFM supplement, not the AIM.
The sources do not say how an instructor and learner, or a safety pilot and pilot, should split the sky into lookout sectors; brief it yourself.
There is no measurable test in the sources for whether a learner's scan is effective; the AIH offers eye-following and questioning, with limits [[25:82|AIH 3-31]] [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

activities.title: Walk the eyes out and back
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the AIM's panel-to-outside scan path in order, then tap Check.
steps: Look out along the left wing, past the tip, to the center of the first scan quadrant
Sweep left to right in moves of 10 degrees or less, at least 1 second per area
Come back into the cabin along the right wing, from its tip inward
activities.why: The AIM path from the panel along the left wing, across, and back along the right wing reduces eye fatigue [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].

activities.title: Read the night scanning drawing
activities.intro: Drag each label to its pin on the drawing.

pins.label: First stop: the greatest distance you can see
End of the far band before moving inward
Last stop, closest to the aircraft
Overlap each new view with the last by 10 degrees

activities.why: Scan side to side, start at the greatest distance and move inward, overlapping each view by 10 degrees [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].

activities.title: Pick the clearing move
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then the clearing procedure that fits it.

pairs.l: High-wing airplane, about to turn left
pairs.r: Momentarily raise the left wing and look

pairs.l: Low-wing airplane, about to turn right
pairs.r: Momentarily lower the right wing and look
Adjust pitch now and then to see over the nose
Break it at intervals with clearing procedures
Scan the approach areas for landing traffic
Clearing turns, calling clear left, right, above and below

activities.why: Wing raise or lower, straight and level, and before takeoff [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f]]; pitch in the climb [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]; verbalized clearing before maneuvers [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

activities.title: Name the scanning limitation
activities.intro: Tap each item, then the AIM limitation group it belongs to.

items.t: Programming the GPS on the tablet
Time to refocus from panel to horizon

activities.why: The AIM groups the limits as reduced scan frequency from instruments, tablets and passengers; blind spots from wings, posts, visors and attitude; weather and the sun; and the eye's own limits such as refocus time and empty-field myopia [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

activities.title: Work the lookout numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Using AC 90-48E Table 1, how many seconds pass from the moment the pilot becomes aware of the collision course (that 5.0 second step is done) until the airplane begins to move?
items.why: Decision to turn 4.0 + muscular reaction 0.4 + aircraft lag 2.0 = 6.4 seconds [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]].

items.q: Using the AIM's lower figure of 4 seconds inside for every 16 seconds outside, how much outside time should go with a 6 second look at the panel?
At the AIM's upper figure (5 seconds inside per 16 outside), what percent of the total time is spent inside? (1 decimal)
items.why: 5 / (5 + 16) = 5 / 21 = 0.238, so 23.8 percent. Compare about 10 percent inside in the AFH's integrated flight instruction [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]] [[24:66|AFH 3-5]].

items.q: Application: the AIM says an aircraft outside foveal vision may not be recognized until it is as close as 7/10 of a mile. Suppose the closure rate is 3 of those same miles per minute. How many seconds remain after the 12.5 second Table 1 time?
items.why: 0.7 / 3 = 0.233 minute x 60 = 14.0 seconds to meet. 14.0 - 12.5 = 1.5 seconds. The 3 miles per minute closure is an assumed example; the AIM does not say whether its miles are statute or nautical, so the closure is given in the same miles [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]] [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]].

items.q: Head-on traffic is 2 NM away at a 200 knot closure. Your learner looks up from the panel (2 seconds to refocus, the AC's upper figure) and then needs the full Table 1 time. How many seconds of margin are left?

activities.title: True or false: teaching the lookout
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In the AIH study, a flight instructor was on board in more than a third of the midair collisions.
If your learner's eyes point at the traffic, you can be sure they saw it.
cards.why: False. Looking in the same direction is not the same as seeing [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

cards.s: Any certificated pilot may act as safety pilot for hood work in an airplane.
cards.why: False. At least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings, with a narrow sport pilot instructor exception [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].

cards.s: TIS-B can show aircraft that have no transponder.
cards.why: False. Only transponder-equipped targets go through the ground system [[33:305|AIM 4-5-8c]].

cards.s: Most midair collisions in the AFH data happen in the morning.
cards.why: False. 56 percent are in the afternoon, 32 percent in the morning [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

cards.s: Dark adaptation is impaired by cabin pressure altitudes above 5,000 feet.

activities.title: A hazy afternoon lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFI for a pre-solo learner in a high-wing trainer. The practice area sits near a VOR, there is a haze layer, and the sun is low in the west.

steps.s: Preflight: the learner plans to work westbound under the haze layer.
options: Cancel the lesson, because scanning cannot work at all in any haze or glare
Go as planned, since visibility meets the legal minimum and the learner can scan normally
Brief glare and haze, and consider working above the haze or with the sun behind you
Plan to rely on the traffic display on the tablet to cover what the haze hides
steps.why: Glare toward the sun hides traffic and haze makes detection hard; the AC recommends flying above haze and planning for the sun [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]] [[16:8|AC 90-48E 9.4]].

steps.s: Taxiing out, the learner starts reading the before-takeoff checklist while rolling.
options: Let it go, since a rolling start saves time and the checklist is short
Read each item aloud while they taxi so their eyes stay mostly outside
Have the learner keep eyes outside and run checklists when stopped
Take over the taxi and finish the checklist yourself while moving
steps.why: Avoid checklists while taxiing; they take attention from scanning [[16:8|AC 90-48E 10.1.2]].

steps.s: In the practice area the learner flies two clearing turns with eyes on the attitude indicator.
options: Point it out and have them repeat the turns looking outside, calling clear left, right, above and below
Accept it, since the turns were flown and the area looked empty on the way out
Fly the clearing turns yourself next time so the learner can watch how it is done
Skip clearing near the VOR since traffic follows the airway and stays on the radial
steps.why: Clearing turns exist to make sure the next maneuver is clear [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]; verbalize them [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15f]], and VORs need sustained vigilance [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15e]].

steps.s: During slow flight you see a low-wing airplane slightly above at 2 o'clock, no relative motion, growing. The learner has not noticed.
options: Wait a few seconds to see whether the learner finds it on their own first
Pull up sharply to pass over it, since it is slightly above you
Point at it and keep teaching so the learner learns to spot it next time
Take the controls, maneuver clear, then have the learner find it
steps.why: No relative motion and growing calls for immediate evasive action [[24:32|AFH 1-11]] [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8e]], and Table 1 needs 12.5 seconds [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]].

steps.s: On the ground the learner asks why they missed it.
options: Tell them to try harder and concentrate more on the scan during the next flight
Explain the low-wing-above-high-wing blind spot and why no relative motion defeats peripheral vision
Blame the haze only and tell them that clear days will not cause this problem
Promise to keep watching for traffic for them until solo, so the learner can concentrate on flying the airplane first
steps.why: A low-wing above a high-wing is the worst case [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]; peripheral vision detects movement [[24:32|AFH 1-11]], and never take over the lookout [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
